We introduce a new concept called a Function Engine (FE), which streamlines the representation and handling of common graphical model messages, including belief propagation (BP), loopy belief propagation (LBP), and the exact inference algorithm (EI). By representing messages as compact function objects rather than bulky data structures, FE enhances efficiency and flexibility. We demonstrate the FE concept by utilizing it to accelerate existing neural message passing inference networks (NemNi) for structured prediction and tree search based on an enhanced negas algorithm. We also present a NMeNi-Con variant of NemNi that incorporates the Function Engine for tree search, enabling constrained optimisation within a graphical model. Our experiments show that FE-based methods consistently outperform traditional NemNi-based approaches in structured prediction under both synthetic and real-world data, and that NMeNi-Con successfully derives feasible solutions for complex communication scenarios.

High-precision measurements through laser spectroscopy and spectroscopy based on cold atoms are complementing each other and offer significant improvements in tests of the standard model and cosmological inquiries. Laser cooling techniques, which rely on absorbing photons, can cool atoms to a very low temperature by selecting the right spectroscopy. Nonetheless, measuring temperatures using the broadening caused by Doppler effects is limited due to its dependence on strong, line-shaping beams, which also induce recoil heating. We demonstrate the transfer of photon momentum to an isolated, unsaturated absorption of a single beam, notably through the spatial separation of atoms that have absorbed a specific wavelength of light. Observing a 40-nm displacement of the absorption feature as a result of the recoil of the atoms allows for a precise measurement of the ratio of the fine-structure and Rydberg constants with an accuracy of 3 parts per billion.

When a suspension experiences sudden shear thickening, it undergoes a transition driven by the competition between fluid inertia and particle pressure inertia. Researchers both theoretically and numerically discovered that this sudden thickening can exist in two forms: one triggered by the balance of shear thinning and pressure inertia (IXP) and the other resulting from the competition between corner rotation and pressure inertia (ICP). However, previous investigations into these phenomena have been primarily static and not explored in the context of complex geometries like the three-way mixing chamber. Our numerical experiments revealed that inertia-driven sudden thickening takes on an abrupt self-nucleating character in intricate shapes, and that the shift from thinning to thickening can be characterized by a universal relation that is independent of the intricate geometry. This implies that despite the geometric complexity, the pressure inertia interplay remains consistent and that a simple mixing chamber can serve a thickening-based pump function.

We establish a connection between the $k$-th generation of a recursive sequence that defines the Racah algebra $R_n$ and the coefficients of a generating function for the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, whose dimension reflects the number of Lie algebra basis elements invariant under conjugation in the group. This document also explores fundamental properties of the Racah algebra, including its relationship with the Hecke algebra, the symmetric group, the Gabrielov permutation, and the Lie algebra, as well as its fundamental realization. We provide an explicit calculation of the associated graded algebra of the centralizer, demonstrating its equivalence to the $n$-th homogeneous component of the Racah algebra, and thereby confirming a historical conjecture about the recursive structure of the Racah algebra and its contribution to the dimension of the centralizer.

Web personalisation is now commonly experienced by users, yet there's little robust empirical data on how personalisation based on past behaviour might lead to missing out on important content in web searches. This study presents two pieces of research that examine this issue - first through web crawl tests with real-world Google searches using the same URLs, and then through a study with actual participants. Surprisingly, our findings show that in some cases, up to 37% of relevant content could be missed just due to web personalisation, even when using the same search engine, on the same device, and accessing the identical web pages. Unfortuntately, an easy way to prevent this issue couldn't be found in our study.

We are investigating how well the discovery capabilities of a 100 TeV muon-based particle collider will match those of its proton equivalents at the same energy level. Specifically, we focus on key physics phenomena such as new heavy particles that could be detected, including the Higgs and top quarks, as well as dark matter and the potential for supersymmetry. Our analysis also considers experiments conducted at colliders with lower energy levels, including 30 and 50 TeV, and both proton and muon-based options. It becomes clear that while proton colliders at the same energy produce heavier particles more easily, their reach is quite comparable in terms of detecting heavy particles associated with the weak force. Consequently, a 50 TeV proton-based collider offers significant advantages over its muon-based 30 TeV counterpart, although the latter still provides substantial discovery potential. In contrast, the 100 TeV muon-based particle shows rivaling the heavy particle production rates of its 50 TeV proton-based predecessor and offers significant unique physics that cannot be duplicated by any lower energy proton-based colliders.

A novel method is proposed to create a four-dimensional (MRI data encompassing motion correction and multiple respiratory depths using the widely applicable T2-weighted sequence. Despite its benefits, traditional TS echoes suffer from artifacts due to their long scan times. To address this issue, the study explores a motion-corrected four-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI approach, leveraging its high speed, short echo time, high resolution, and broad coverage. Experiments conducted on four living subjects demonstrate that our method successfully recovers scan areas affected by diaphragmatic compression. Additionally, the study shows that a narrow bandwidth setting yields narrower peak broadening than the standard setting. The results indicate that a full k-space readout setting produces narrower peaks and better resolution compared to a partial k-space readout setting. The reconstructed images exhibit sharp boundaries, a high signal-to-noise ratio, and sufficient resolution. The study estimates that a respiratory navigation approach requires approximately 3.5 times the duration of a free-breathing scan. The reconstructed images demonstrate full anatomical coverage without areas of missing data. A four-dimensional dataset with motion correction is produced, enabling accurate, automatic segmentation and the extraction of a single, high-quality image at each respiratory stage.

The paired-permutation test is a statistical method used to determine the relevance of features. However, the extensive size of the permutation space makes it difficult to accurately assess the relevance of features through permutations. In response to this challenge, a paired-rewiring approach was developed to generate permutations that preserve the sum of a statistic calculated on the data rows. This strategy enables precise p-values for test statistics in forms such as linear regression sums, and allows for efficient computation of permutations in polynomial time relative to the sample size. Moreover, the paired-permutation test can be utilized to select important components in machine learning models, and a demonstration of its effectiveness can be seen in the training of a classifier with a support vector machine.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping volumes, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled for the global container shipping industry from 1966 to the present, with accompanying statistics describing each variable's underlying structure.

We establish a loom theory for veering triangulations, extending a previous framework developed by the author and K. Margalit. This extension clarifies that every non-trivial loom area decomposition corresponds uniquely to a specific type of triangulation on a surface. In the case of a once-punctured torus, this once-provisional loom model can be transformed into a complete ideal triangulation through the application of local cutting and pasting techniques.

The recent interest in the financial market has also extended to the interest in predicting the future of the market. This research focuses on automating the prediction of the US stock market's value by utilizing state-of-the-art deep learning models. A random forest classifier was employed to handle missing values, followed a BERT-based regression system to establish the relationship between various factors and the stock market value. Since there was sometimes the need to make the best possible predictions, a generative adversarial network was used in addition. This study involves using financial data from 44 US companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange between 2011 and 2019. The results show that a combination of a BERT system and a generative adversarial network can accurately forecast the US stock market value and the value of individual stocks between the years 2018 and 2019. This research also compares its findings a to a BERT system, generative adversarial network, and a random forest classifier in terms of performance.

We investigate the potential for detecting new physics in HH$\gamma\gamma$ events, occurring via tree level, at TeV scale $e^+e^-$ colliders with a 1 Tb inverse luminosity. Focus is placed on the HH$\gamma\gamma$ channel and a broader study of double Higgs production with hadronic decays, to enhance our comprehension of HH signal within the predicted range. In half a year of operation at 500 GeV with the FCC-ee or 3 years at 3 TeV with the CLIC, models beyond the Standard Model for the Higgs sector will be tightly constrained. With an effective field theory framework, coefficients of the Higgs operator basis will be limited to within the 0.1 pb cross-section with 500 GeV and 0.05 pb with 3 TeV.

We modify the conventional kinetic term for matter fields in the Standard Model, replacing it with a Nambu-Bjorker-type formulation. By utilizing a symbolic computation tool, we derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for this formulation and confirm its equivalence to the standard theory. After validating these findings with a simplified scalar field model, we demonstrate that our approach yields an identical result.

We investigated the drag experienced by long cylindrical objects moving within granular material, where the grain size is significantly smaller than the cylinder's diameter. The drag coefficients for these objects were found to vary based on the angle of its long axis relative to the direction of movement, a phenomenon we attribute to the accumulation of material around the cylinder's ends. The relationship between the drag and this angle changes depending on whether the grain size is very small or comparable to the cylinder's diameter. The behavior of these objects is also influenced by the angle of internal friction of the underlying granular material, as well as its internal packing density.

Our research examines the predictions of a multiphase transport model for initial anisotropic flow, specifically the triangular flow ($v_3$), across a spectrum of heavy-ion collisions, including Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various energies. By analyzing the initial anisotropic flow, we can gain insights into the quark-gluon plasma's properties. Notably, we discovered an elevated average value of elliptical flow coefficient in comparison to eccentricity-based findings. However, we found the predicted triangular flow values to be in line with experimental data. A non-negligible value of the triangular flow was observed beyond the transition region where collisions produce quark-gluon plasma. Since the initial anisotropic flow is intrinsically linked to thermal fluctuations, we found the supersaturation pressure to be in excellent agreement with extracted values from measured initial anisotropic flow.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in non-leptonic beauty meson decay and CP-violating processes. This section delves into recent discoveries and findings from the ATLAS collaboration concerning these processes, specifically the decay of $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and determining the weak phase associated with this decay.

A critical issue with precision loss in solving linear systems arising from structure-preserving discretization methods, such as symplectic, monotone, and energy-conserving schemes, is explored in this paper. We examine the underlying causes of this problem and develop remedies based on preconditioners within the same numerical scheme's framework. The effectiveness of our approaches is demonstrated through numerical experiments involving Hamiltonian systems and fluid dynamics simulations of the Euler equations.

A significant challenge in medical image analysis is performing a precise and consistent volume-to-surface registration between a postoperative image and a preoperative surface model. This task is especially complicated by tissue deformation occurring following a surgical procedure. To address this challenge, our goal is to develop a robust and computationally efficient method for postoperative volume-to-preoperative surface alignment automatically. Our approach accurately reconstructs a distorted field of view image by utilizing a realistic, patient-specific biomechanical model that accounts for the effects of surgery on the visual field. The model, enhanced with a novel, efficient algorithm for parameter optimization, utilizes a variety of forces including corner markers, elastic forces, and attractive forces to guide the simulation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurate and automatic surface reconstruction for this challenging scenario in real-world clinical settings.

Determining scene flow in a dynamic environment proves to be a challenging task. Our innovation in addressing this problem is MetriFlow32, a novel self-supervised metric learning framework. MetriFlow32 leverages aggregate flow metrics to distinguish similar frame sequences and separates distinct sequences, integrating 2D metric learning into the task. However, we discovered that standard training methods lead to a model that distinguishes only a subset of pairs, yielding poor results in practical applications. In this study, we explore various enhancements to this basic approach and introduce a unified framework that combines instance, point, and quadrant pairs within our method. We utilize the learned metric space for a wide range of applications, including novel testing scenarios, and develop an innovative application-specific module for scene flow estimation. When combined, our advancements lead to significant gains over the state-of-the-art results on the KITTI and SVO datasets.

Classifying complex data patterns efficiently using artificial neural networks is an intriguing challenge in the field of neuromorphic technology. Although Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an advantageous alternative to conventional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in specific scenarios, the current potential of these networks has not been fully realized due to limited understanding of their capabilities. An initial approach in this research involves developing a Class-Selective Spiking Neural Network (CS-SNN) that draws upon the benefits of both random neural networks and simple classification techniques. By leveraging pre-computed features that are common to data within the same class, the model reduces the need for energy-intensive comparisons with other classes to just using a lookup table. Experimental results from an image classification task demonstrate that this novel approach can achieve the same level of performance as traditional methods while significantly improving speed and reducing costs by up to two orders of magnitude on an analog neural processor. However, the research also highlights the restricted applicability of this initial approach in applications with diverse data classes, prompting the creation of a more sophisticated version that combines the advantages of the first approach in specific cases while introducing a novel two-stage learning process with significantly enhanced efficiency.

The structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars is investigated in environments with high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. In this research, a new equation of state is developed within the framework of quantum chromodynamics using an ANE effective Lagrangian in both its vacuum and thermally excited states, including the effects of temperature and a strong magnetic field. The resulting equations for a star are combined with temperature-based equation of state within the relativistic 3K framework. It is found that thermal and strong magnetic fields influence the behavior of quark stars, modifying their thermal pressure, quark number density, and energy density. Notably, an increase in the magnetic field temperature leads to the formation of fully polarized quark stars.

We consider a specific subclass of cubic graphs that exclude 3-cycles. A well-known result proves that any graph containing a particular structure - the Petersen graph as a minor. According to a theorem from Wagner in 1937. For graphs in this class that also lack a Petersen graph as a minor, we can confirm the existence of a perfect matching outside of any cycle of length greater than a certain threshold, as established in 1961. This enables us to colour the edges of these graphs using only three colours, extending a property first observed by Tait in 1880. These findings expand on earlier research.

Containerized applications offer significant flexibility and speed in developing and deploying software. To further enhance this process, our new tool called Timeloops automatically learns call dependencies among system components using reinforcement reasoning. Applied to an actual autonomous trading platform, Timeloops discovered critical call sequences that prevented trading delays of up to 110 percent, improving overall system speed by 27 percent on average.

This study develops a filtering method for a dynamic set of points within a defined area. In an attempt to streamline the computational process, a new approach is introduced to determine the birth probability within a specific region. A particular application of this technique in sensor management is examined. Consequently, the problem of decison making for data acquisition is tackled for an effective sensor that can make instant measurements outside a predefined area. A optimal filter is derived in the form of a Partially Amplitude Belman Equation. In order to apply this in practice, it linearizes and Gaussianizes the model of birth, resulting in the incorporation of the birth update into the standard PDAI filter. Simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in real-world scenarios.

This research examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior decay term and a diffusion process. By selecting an appropriate control area, we demonstrate that it's possible to steer the population to zero in a finite amount of time. An interesting finding arises in the case of unlimited growth potential, revealing that steering the population to zero is also feasible within its natural habitat. Furthermore, we extend our results to a broader class of growth functions. An accompanying paper develops explicit ways to achieve null controllability for this population model.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small advantages can lead to scoring goals, making the final result highly unpredictable. Established research highlights various factors contributing to this uncertainty, including instances where players have taken drastic actions in the aftermath of critical errors, such as ramming balls into players or deliberately destroying the goalpost. Although these events are extraordinary and difficult to forecast, this study aims to explore and quantify unusual actions in the case of soccer mistakes to provide valuable inputs for future simulations involving soccer agents. To accomplish this, we collected real-world data from professional soccer games, focusing on post-incident actions performed by players who had witnessed a critical error. We examined several factors including the incident type, a player's own involvement, their position on the field, and their proximity to the event. Notably, our findings show that players have often engaged in self-harmful or self-endangering actions following such incidents. Furthermore, contrary to commonly held beliefs, our results indicate that self-sabotaging actions were frequently performed by players with sports training, those playing near the ball, goalkeepers, and players situated close to the event site. To accommodate these discoveries, we introduced a modified version of the state-space for our deep reinforcement learning-based soccer simulator, and found that the altered model required significantly fewer simulation steps to accurately replicate actual behaviors.

Based on recent progress, hypernovae and neutron star mergers are now understood as multi-messenger sources, providing enriched information compared to traditional electromagnetic observations alone. Although the point source assumption holds for the late stages of neutron star mergers, the extension to hypernovae with wide jet openings necessitates accounting for the source's geometry. This paper presents the first signal inversion framework for hypernova jet structures, demonstrating successful reconstruction of a simulated long gamma-ray burst event, including its jet structure. By integrating gravitational wave, high-energy, and astronomical imaging data, constraining hypernova parameters is anticipated to be possible in the future, thereby deepening our understanding of the nuclear force and general relativity.

A novel stochastic spatial model was developed to simulate the election process of a partisan election involving multiple candidates, with the balance between local competition and distant colony formation influencing the outcome, where the species with the advantage in colonizing new areas doesn't always end up dominating the entire habitat, and various stable configurations of dominant species can exist across different parts of the environment.

An integrated data and energy network (IDEN) incorporates a cognitive radio element and uses a reflectarray to transfer data and supplement the power grid. Coexistence with nearby device-to-device (D2D) interference is managed by dynamically adjusting the reflectarray configuration. A key constraint is set to prevent D2D signals from degrading beyond an acceptable level. The aim is to maximize the IDEN's data transfer capacity while considering the presence of D2D communications. Initially, an optimal reflectarray configuration is determined to allow for the highest data transfer at a specific D2D activity level. Subsequently, in a more complex scenario where D2D activity fluctuates, a set of configurations is established. One of these configurations is then selected based on the current D2D activity to manage interference in real-time. This approach also leads to a set of side benefits, including a method to limit D2D activity to its minimum necessary level, in order to achieve the same data transfer and reflectarray performance.

Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) is widely used in fluid dynamics research due to its high-resolution, non-invasive velocity measurements. As the LDV system's working distance varies, it can accommodate different measurement scenarios; however, extending the working distance often presents challenges, especially for large-scale facilities where instruments must reach distant surfaces. This is where reach modules come in, enabling the LDV system to cover greater distances; nevertheless, existing modules require significant data acquisition times for LIF imaging. In response, a newly designed reach module with a shortened working distance of 4 meters is presented, demonstrating the feasible acquisition of label-free 2D measurements at extended ranges. Utilizing a high-frequency LDV system, the proposed method successfully acquired velocity contours around an airfoil without encountering signal-to-noise ratio challenges. Furthermore, the LDV system's capability to measure guided acoustic-modeled airflow in a rectangular duct was also exhibited. These findings indicate the potential for acquiring labeled or unlabeled flow field images using LDV on various flow field scales; however, this relies on the appropriate surface preparation when using fluorescent particles.

The performance of Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) is hindered by electron lens defects, which cause image errors. Correcting these defects traditionally involves specialized, unchangeable devices, but a novel, programmable phase plate is proposed that could adapt to different lens systems by changing its error patterns via a computer, potentially functioning as both a corrector and standard phase plate, albeit facing technical obstacles for implementation in TEMs.

We derive new results regarding the structure of certain types of quadratic extensions, specifically integral modules over the ring of endomorphisms of Q with a set of coefficients. Building on previous work, we establish conditions for an integral module to have a specific property, known as a strong set of coefficients, which is closely related to the ability to approximate certain numbers using an equivalent form of physics known as a leopoldt's form. This enhancement of a theorem originally proven by leopoldt has practical significance for an algorithm developed by ray in determining whether two number systems are actually the same. We also discuss the application of this concept of a leopoldt-type property to determining whether two number systems are identical.

In experiments conducted with Belle II, searching for axion-like particles involves analyzing missing mass distributions in processes where a charmonium particle decays into a photon and an undetected particle. A study focusing on two such processes, $J/\psi \to \gamma X$ and $\psi' \to \gamma X$, identifies specific energy ranges for these decays. To explore a broader spectrum, other $B$ meson decay paths such as $B^0 \to \gamma X$, $B^+\to \gamma X$, and $B^+\to e^+\gamma X$ are suggested as they expand the range of masses that can be probed to roughly 0.1 to 3.6~GeV. Given the large number of disallowed regions, even a modest BelII data set allows researchers to set stringent limits on the interaction of these particles with photons, potentially offering a significant improvement over existing standards.

Recent advances in semantic alteration detection have been facilitated by the integration of contextualized language models. Since the precise mechanism these models should be tuned to identify alterations remains unclear, we examined various approaches by testing multiple configurations, thresholds, and component combinations for seven distinct tasks. Notably, we developed an open-source dataset consisting of 1 million text pairs to support research in this area. Moreover, we explored the potential for cross-task generalization using several contextually-aware methods.

When a heavy particle moves at a relativistic speed, its intrinsic angular momentum, or spin, behaves like a detector for any fundamental attributes of particles, including dark matter. This has given rise to three distinct mechanisms based on the size of spatial scales relative to the Compton wavelength. Two of these mechanisms, parametric resonance and vacuum instability, were recently identified and could potentially be detected using heavy cosmic objects such as pulsars, planetary nebulae, and radio galaxies. However, by focusing on the scales of these objects, previous models of interactions fail to capture the behavior of extremely light particles, especially those interacting with atomic electrons. By developing a unified framework that combines general relativity, quantum field theory, and plasma physics, we can assess the feasibility of detecting unique phenomena, including the formation of axion clouds around heavy quasas and oscillating vacuum bubbles, which may produce observable effects such as variations in particle masses and anomalous emissions of electromagnetic radiation. These predictions could be testable with next-generation telescopes like the Extremely Large Telescope and the Chinese 100-meter telescope, as well as existing observatories such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

A distinctive feature of neuroblast development is the rhythmic migration of nuclei across the retinal layer during interkinetic nuclear movement, which starts in early developmental stages and retires as cells prepare for division. Though it's happening while cells are not dividing, its purpose remains unclear. Through the formulation of a conserved division pattern that maximizes efficiency, our model suggests that this movement helps optimize the placement of dividing neuroblasts. To test this, we developed a high-resolution, live-retina tracking method and performed a detailed analysis of motion in the zebrafish retina, revealing its random-walk-like nature. Furthermore, we discovered that areas with higher cell density exhibit less movement, indicating that this is largely governed by contact inhibition. In summary, our investigation integrates process breakdown, an ecological context, and a proposed function for the Zebrafish retina's interkinetic nuclear movement.

In modern video and image processing pipelines, multiple processes like compression, sensing, and noise often lead to intertwined issues, making advanced modeling of their combined effects along with intelligent optimization of codes for better performance a new and exciting area of study. Using a realistic video recovery scenario involving compression, random sensor patterns, and unknown mixing, we created an in-depth generative model for Compressively Intertwined Video Recovery (CIVR). Our novel approach includes a latent code that captures code-shareable information beneficial for both reconstruction accuracy and model generalization to other sensing patterns. Due to its enhanced capability, our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art method on a real-world video recovery dataset with a significant improvement in reconstruction accuracy by nearly 20%. Furthermore, we found that incorporating our code in a color image demosaicing task resulted in a notable performance gain of around 5%. These outcomes highlight the importance of developing integrative models and optimized codes for a more accurate and adaptable source separation in video and image processing applications. Our code is available online at this URL: https://github.com/yuxiangli99/civr_source_separation.

We provide an analytically simplified model of incompressible polar active fluids in the presence of quenched velocity field defects across $d$ spatial dimensions ($d>2$). Through a self-consistent approach, we investigate the typical dynamics of this system, revealing the presence of a characteristic wave number $k^*$ that separates two distinct regimes. Wave numbers larger than $k^*$ exhibit localized typical dynamics, while smaller wave numbers demonstrate delocalized typical dynamics. Our findings are visually demonstrated using phase portraits generated through large-scale simulations of the Swinney-Turnbull model of incompressible polar active fluids. A customized spectral time-integration algorithm is employed to simulate this model, and the results are visually represented using high-resolution three-dimensional renderings.

We will demonstrate the application of the path integral approach to solve the harmonic oscillator problem with a driving force by calculating the propagator via Metropolis-Hastings and Hybrid Monte Carlo simulations of a suitable imaginary time configuration model. Next we will show how to compute the probability distribution of certain features of typical paths within this distribution. Furthermore, we'll show how to derive the driving-force-dependent expectation and variance of the position.

The YORP effect causes asteroids to experience temperature differences across their surfaces, which in turn leads to a measurement of their rotation speeds. This paper delves into the statistics of the YORP effect and utilizes maximum-likelihood methods to analyze observations of asteroids, facilitating an examination of how their initial rotation speeds impact the YORP effect's ability to be measured. Focus is placed on the asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, which have had their shape models refined and had surface features mapped, which could potentially allow for the theory of the YORP effect to be validated by comparing it to the observed "sun-synchronous" orbits of these asteroids, once the distributions of their surface temperatures are calculated through radiometric observations.

We demonstrate that the group of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, denoted as $\operatorname{Home}_0(S)$, when restricted to any substantial subset, contains a collection of functions whose graphs have the same approximate size as the surface, and exhibit the characteristic of not being compact under the Roelcke topology.

We extend a computable version of Thomsen's finite automata construction, originally a modification of Kleene's work, by establishing a corresponding relationship between finite state automata and infinite word systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that every deterministic co-B\"{u}chi automaton defines a computable language through infinite words. Additionally, we investigate the properties of determinizable co-B\"{u}chi automata defining infinite word languages and describe the characteristics of such languages.

In our study, we investigate a simplified model of two competing species, accounting for various delays in the system. By extending the parameter space with multiple dimensions, we map out the parameters that define the system's behavior. We then focus on a specific area with complicated dynamics and identify regions where two competingattractor states coexist. Using linkedattractor techniques, we distinguish and categorize different configurations in this area, which we visualize in an extensive graphic representation. We further explore the system's dynamics by examining the distribution and coexistence ofattractor states.

We develop a second-order numerical method for calculating the reachability set S that results from a control input u belonging to Uad and is influenced by another variable v belonging to Vad, for a given time T. Our approach, which is grounded in a first-order result established in a previous study, achieves a precision of OT^(3/2) + O(Vad^(3/2)) in the L1 norm, where O() denotes a constant, T and Vad represent the time step and the spatial step size, respectively. Our numerical scheme, which is based on a discrete Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, is robust to changes in step size and remains effective in high dimensions. Our approach is validated through numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional case with a complex domain.

The ventral temporal cortex, a crucial component of the human brain, is where visual input is processed and converted into a more comprehensive understanding.  According to a new hypothesis, this area is fundamentally organized based on whether entities are living or non-living.  This proposed fundamental status of animacy is supported by three key arguments: evidence showing that the effects of animacy in the brain are unchanged over time, differences in the impact of animacy on different types of living entities, and an comparison between the impact of animacy and other categories that are less significant in humans but in animals.  Furthermore, this perspective is connected to other research that has found that the animacy boundary in the brain is linked to the separation between faces, places, and objects, as well as the intricate neural patterns in the temporal lobe that reflect the complexity of the animacy distinction.

There is a quantum version of unique ergodicity for the group PGL_3(Q) acting on PGL_3(R)\PGL_3(K), where K is either the real numbers or a specific quadratic field. A key researcher, Iwaniec, proposed that this quantum unique ergodicity holds for all closed subgroups within PGL_3(R)\PGL_3(K). Our work builds on Iwaniec's quantum unique ergodicity conjecture by showing it holds with efficiency for the specific group, also known as Hecke-Siegel zeros existing efficiently.

We extend Quantum Relational Hoare Reasoning with partial and quantum expectations to enable the comparison of two programs' output. These programs may differ in how they handle input and produce potentially different outcomes on behalf of the observer. Our framework encompasses traditional correctness properties like standard equality and refinement in addition to new properties not previously supported, such as linear correctness, differential safety, and capacity reduction, among others, all within a unified approach based on quantum mechanics and partially lost information represented by expectations.

Recent studies highlighting the significance of "super-spreading" events has attracted considerable interest.  To better understand the influence of such events, we developed a comprehensive database drawing from various open sources of information, and found that around 30 to 50% of new infections and deaths during the COVID-19 pandemic were directly linked to high-transmission events. These findings were then applied to a synthetic population to assess the potential for modeling high-transmission scenarios. We found that models lacking super-spreading events fail to accurately replicate the high-tail distributions seen in cumulative infection data. However, the spatial spread of diseases is less significantly affected by such events compared to cumulative statistics, and we observed similar results from both randomly and geographically localized super-spreading events. The critical role models play in forecasting the course of epidemics was recently highlighted, and high-transmission events is one of the most high-profile aspects that many current models fail to represent.

Let's consider a pair consisting of a complex topological vector space, X, and a collection of continuous linear operators on X, denoted as $\mathcal A$. If there exists a finite set of non-zero complex numbers that, when used to multiply the operators in $\mathcal A$ in some order and added together, result in the identity operator on X, then $\mathcal A$ is said to be cyclic. 

This paper aims to characterize the sets of operators $\mathcal A$ which are guaranteed to be cyclic, provided certain vectors in X are specified. It is shown that if the set of operators $\mathcal A$ is both algebraically dense within the algebra of all operators on X and commutative, then it is necessarily cyclic. Moreover, a broader condition of hyper reflexivity is introduced to provide a more rigorous criterion for ensuring the cyclicity of the set of operators $\mathcal A$. 

The results discussed build upon a previous finding by Koliada and Shemchuk (2019).

The Stokes polarization data, which form the basis for vector magnetic field measurements in the sun, are susceptible to bias in their inferred quantities, especially in regions with complex magnetic field configurations. Researchers normally assume that the distributions of these inferred quantities are Gaussian and use their statistics to identify outliers. However, as this study demonstrates, these distributions are highly skewed and contain significant systematic errors that can be misinterpreted as field anomalies. Moreover, observational techniques such as Maximum Likelihood Estimators and Median filters, which depend on these statistics, may filter healthy magnetic features or pass truly anomalous ones. By developing mock observations and applying them to a simple holographic instrument model, this research effectively captures the distribution characteristics seen in real data. It also reveals that a post-processing step, which leverages the relationship between total magnetic field strength and the largest component in active region spots, can correct the inferred quantities to closely resemble Gaussian distributions, effectively improving the reliability of such quantities for detecting solar magnetic anomalies.

Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) simulations, a key component of many electron systems' full variational approaches, generally produce a form that guarantees the ground state's particle-hole symmetry. However, this DMC phase often becomes intractably large, scaling exponentially with the size of the system, and can impede problem solvability in certain cases, particularly when there are multiple ways to satisfy the Dyson symmetry. A proposed solution involves utilizing a simplified sign-free variant, finding that the complexity manages to scale much more gracefully than its original, exhaustive version. Our investigation utilizes the lightweight, contractive Dyson phase to demonstrate this method's effectiveness and efficiency, employing classical and quantum simulations to assess performance and network size optimizations for a 2D filled-band Hubbard model. Our findings show that the sign-free version can successfully tackle problem sizes up to at least (32,32), and possibly beyond, on modest hardware.

Given two free subsemigroups S and T within a free semigroup F, we examine a semigroup homomorphism h that maps the generation sets of S and T. For subsemigroups S, if they are recognized by a regular language, we establish that topological entropy remains unchanged under the homomorphism h, providing an additive relationship involving the images of the generation sets of S. Similarly, the topological complexity and PL-complexity satisfy linear combinations based on the dimensions of the preimages under the homomorphism. For subsemigroups S with a parabolic growth property, the topological entropy of their free group completion also adheres to the same additive rule.

Due to the convenience and cost-effectiveness of large language models, numerous task-specific annotation sets have been produced.
In situations where sufficient resources allow, combining diverse datasets can enable promising results on individual tasks.
However, when only limited resources are available for training, a single model tends to become specialized in one task and struggles to generalize effectively across multiple tasks in unsupervised cross-task scenarios.
Our research focuses on this unsupervised cross-task generalization limitation.
We propose a lightweight, user-tailored approach known as Retrieval Enhancement Training (RET), in which another model selects data samples from across diverse datasets, eschewing any label-based exclusion, and using this selectively assembled training set yields improved cross-task performance.
RET's successful performance is attributed to its ability to mimic a idealized cross-task prior and its implicit utilization of task identity information.
Our proposed method's effectiveness is further bolstered by integrating a simple retrieval loss, demonstrating retargetable cross-task generalization.
RET's advantages are additionally highlighted by its implicit utilization of task identity information.
Our proposed method's effectiveness is further demonstrated in unsupervised cross-task settings.

Machine-learning models trained with privately protected algorithms offer improved user data privacy but present a challenging optimization problem due to its stochastic and distribution-less nature. In the realm of deep learning, this problem is further compounded by the need to efficiently search for optimal parameters. This study proposes a private hyperspace efficient method, leveraging the Global Average Pooling aggregation technique and a large-scale parameter search enabled by Swag for uncertainty estimation. By incorporating these innovations, a feasible parameter search is made possible within reasonable timeframes. The proposed technique is successfully applied to multiple tasks, including image and text-based classification, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness.

Involutions within a symmetric group S_n form a complex shape that can't be described as a simple arrangement, consisting of four distinct components: intervals within the Coxeter arrangement, consisting of functions related to a specific number of points in a sequence. Notably, these components relate to the number of points in a sequence that correspond to the involution's fixed points.

A comprehensive analysis of 1432 chemical elements in 420 stars from the APOGEE-2 project was conducted, focusing on stars with ages exceeding five billion years. To interpret these detailed observations, two external modeling approaches were utilized: a initial method calculated each element's abundance based on five conditions (metallicity, carbon content, gravity, rotation, and angular velocity), but complex patterns required; subsequently, a more intricate model was created that matched the remaining variations in abundance. Both approaches indicated that the stars belong to distinct population groups with unique characteristics: one group with normal to low angular velocity, and another with high carbon content. Furthermore, previous research findings were verified, and unusual anomalies in calculated patterns allowed for a calculation of the angular velocity for five of the studied stars.

A custom mathematical model based on a spread equation is proposed to analyze the COVID-19 pandemic news in China, focusing on distinguishing between legitimate news and rumors online. The model's parameters have physical meanings and can be directly derived from data, providing a convenient way to measure the influence of variables on the development of public opinion without using complex statistical methods. A case study reveals that a key factor is not constant over time and varies depending on the period, leading to different outcomes in the formation of public opinion. The spread equation method outperforms existing statistical models in predicting news topic trends. Combining this method with the SIR model offers valuable insights for understanding the characteristics of viral news and rumors, highlighting the need for in-depth analysis beyond conventional statistical approaches.

A novel approach to estimating the distance to galaxy clusters by comparing measured distances to planetary nebulae with their simulated distribution has yielded promising results for the Fornax cluster. Previous studies individually determined the distances to over 2000 planetary nebulae within six galaxies of the cluster using the $c/n$ ratio method. In an attempt to enhance precision, a study rebased the individual measurements, accounting for systematic errors, to create a unified planetary nebulae sample. When compared to accepted distance estimates, such as those from the rotation curve of the dwarf spiral galaxy LGQ-604, a initial finding suggested an unusually wide range of distances for the cluster. A subsequent analysis, however, refined the calculated distances to the galaxies based on their morphological type, resulting in a narrower, more conventional distance range of 16.5 to 19.0 Mpc. A critical asset of this study is the compilation of a comprehensive planetary nebulae database for the six galaxies, which includes their $c/n$ ratios, $\log (c/n)$ values, and their previously measured distances in Mpc. Furthermore, a separate analysis of the $c/n$ ratio distribution for each of the six galaxies was presented. The previously measured distances to the galaxies and the planetary nebulae directory are publicly accessible.

Traditional stream processing systems struggle with the escalating demands of big data, especially when dealing with periodic datasets containing thousands of relations. These systems' static nature makes adapting to the varying sizes of input streams difficult and inefficient. In contrast, our new flow-based engine, LifeStream, is statically designed to handle the growth of stream sizes with efficiency. It enables the creation of complex stream programs that are both high-performance and easy to deploy. Moreover, life programs are inherently robust, statically well-typed, and come with guaranteed properties like dataflow preservation. The Stg2Flow translation algorithm transforms these stage2 stage flow programs into statically typed flow graphs that are dynamically adaptable to the sizes of input streams while maintaining optimal performance. Our experimental results show significant improvements in speed and scalability, with life programs transforming 10,000 stream programs of sizes up to 10 million records in under a second, and achieving up to an order of magnitude better performance compared to the ocaml streaming library. The engine's transformation rate can also be further optimized to the hundreds of millions.

Using a specific type of geometric space called a semi-metric space, we've demonstrated that certain time-oriented curves, specifically Bertrand curves, can only take on a particular shape with constant properties under very limited conditions.

The choice of loss function in classification tasks is well-established, but for neural networks, alternatives exist that may have unexplored implications. This research investigates how loss functions based on probability and those on decision boundaries compare, utilizing both theoretical analysis and deep learning. Through mathematical derivation, we found that for linear classifiers and convex loss functions, the two approaches yield the same result. However, non-convex functions, commonly used in deep learning, have been demonstrated to lead to potentially divergent outcomes. A practical experiment was also conducted to further validate these findings, and it supported the hypothesis that the choice of loss function can have significant impacts. As a consequence of these results, it is advisable to carefully consider the underlying assumptions of the loss function in conjunction with the model, and to test multiple loss functions to optimize performance.

This research aims to advance the simulation of polymer crystallization induced by strain. The process involves the expansion of thin, needle-like structures within stretched polymers, resulting in significant material instability. Our model accounts for the mechanical behavior and thermal properties of polymers during their transition from liquid to solid states. It integrates a crystallization thermodynamics approach with finite element methods to solve balance equations for mass, momentum, and energy. The simulation incorporates the generation and consumption of heat during phase transformation. Initially, the model was tested on planar elongation simulations using a polyethylene model, revealing that even minor levels of tension can lead to rapid, self-sustaining crystal growth. The findings were visually represented through time-lapse sequences and cross-sectional analyses. However, the simulation reveals unrealistically sharp transitions between crystal and molten states. The limitations of the strain-induced crystallization model were identified, highlighting the need for further research to develop more sophisticated simulations capable of capturing the full range of structural changes in polymers under tension.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on a nematic $T_2$-wave superconductor, we studied two distinct regimes. Initially, the magnetic field strength was found to create three sub-bands within the superconductor. A perturbation theory was applied to a specific part of the dispersion relation to discover that a Pauli triplet occurs at the extremum of a sub-band under a specific nematicity condition. Subsequently, we applied the Dyson equation to demonstrate that the self-energy's anisotropy leads to the anisotropy of the superconductor's critical temperature. Under the Nernst effect, an anisotropy in the critical temperature results in an anisotropy in the generated voltage. Consequently, the induced Nernst effect is observed as a pair of opposite signs in a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. Under a second scenario where the magnetic field strength is large compared to the superconductor's pairing potential, Pauli paramagnetism of the Cooper couples in the superconducting state is found to be enhanced.

A widely used digital differential continuous-phase modulation (DCPM) detection technique, the $q$-delay method, is examined in this study, and an improvement is proposed to improve its performance. The modification keeps the differential detection's byte timing advantage while reducing required memory and increasing the benefit in that regard. Modified versions of common DCPM techniques, including GMSK and $\pi$/2 DCPM, are studied in detail, and simulation results are presented to compare the method with a alternative detection strategy in detail.

A previous paper suggested using fluctuating thermal radiation to establish a quantum communication link across space. To assess this proposal, the quantum reliability of spacetime was found to be equivalent to the Blum-Roberts capacity of spacetime's transfer matrix, which was demonstrated to behave like a system with multiple inputs and outputs, influenced by the temperatures of surrounding thermal radiators. A simplified model was also developed to visualize the factors limiting radiators' contributions to this system.

Large-scale artificial intelligence systems often struggle with reasoning abilities, particularly when it comes to drawing conclusions based on conditional statements. These statements, although simple and often seen as unproblematic, actually require a comprehensive understanding of subject matter and the identification of causal links. In this study, we introduce the ATOMIC atlas, consisting of over 1.3 million if-then reasoning pairs within a single domain and 135 thousand entries across multiple domains. This structure enables enhanced learning in individual fields as well as the integration of diverse subject matter. Our research shows that the ATOMIC atlas significantly improves the performance of various AI-based reasoning models, especially when comparing it to using just text definitions. Moreover, we discovered that graphical representations and tabular formats play a crucial role in strengthening hypothesized human intelligence components and allowing for a systematic evaluation of subject matter importance and the necessity of if-then reasoning.

Quantum computing's prospects in finance are being thoroughly explored, with highlights such as the McKinsey and McKinsey Reports highlighting various applications and strategies. Despite their general nature, these reports do not specifically address how to effectively use quantum hardware in a short and imperfect timeframe. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of potential quantum hardware applications in financial management. It further introduces a specific application: optimizing investment portfolios through multi-objective reinforcement learning to train a portfolio allocation network. This network manages investment portfolios by adjusting parameters of the Hayashi-Kubo-Harada's algorithm. It is demonstrated that combining reinforcement learning with the HHL algorithm results in a significant performance improvement on actual quantum hardware. Moreover, this research reveals that delaying the execution of certain parts of the HHL algorithm through pre- and post-processing techniques can lead to a significant reduction in computational costs and a substantial enhancement in solution accuracy. Ultimately, this strategy is shown to significantly improve accuracy when applying the HHL algorithm to real quantum hardware.

We present a unified multi-modal learning approach for enhancing speech
recognition, initially with a basic approach and subsequently incorporating advanced
technology. In the multi-modal framework, the system makes efforts to align
alternating speech and text data for a unified understanding. We utilize a
state-of-the-art text-based model pre-trained with bidirectional attention (BiAttn)
and incorporate a bi-directional attention mechanism that allows the model to
focus selectively on past or future speech content. We denote this approach as
BioTrn. Our experiments utilizing BioTrn in actual applications demonstrate
significant improvements in addition to facilitating a broader range of
applications.

Let $f_n$ be a randomly selected parking function from the $n$-th set of parking functions. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the first position in the sequence $f_n$, denoted as $\mathbb{E}\left(\text{first}(f_n)\right)$, for large values of $n$. For a comprehensive understanding of parking functions and their properties, references are provided in references 1, 2, and 3. Based on an existing result from literature (reference 1), it is shown that the expected first position grows at a rate between $n^{.5}$ and $n$ and is tightly bounded. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for a specific subset of parking functions, defined as superfunctions (reference 5), the rate of growth is between $n^{.75}$ and $n$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the rate of growth is between $n^{.75}$ and $n$. However, it is also found that when considering monotonically increasing parking functions, denoted as $\pi_n$, the rate of first position growth is bounded between $n^{.4}$ and $n$.

Investigations of superconducting nanowires often revolve around two main phenomena: granular nanowires exhibit a combination of Josephson junctions and Josephson plasma modes, while clean nanowires display coherent quantum phase slips that can lead to an insulating state. To study these effects cleanly, we propose using a semiconductor field-effect transistor to control the charge neutrality point in nanowires made of NbN. By doing so, we can avoid artifacts caused by trapped charges and interface defects. In this paper, we investigate NbN nanowires both with and without a gate, comparing our results to theoretical predictions and previous studies. We observe that as we approach the critical point, the resistance increases linearly rather than following a quadratic relationship seen in other studies. We attribute the resistance increase to localized states near the neutrality point, and conclude that our data do not strongly indicate that quantum phase slips occur in dirty superconducting nanowires at zero temperature.

A major hurdle in generating videos for novel viewpoints arises from the ambiguous nature of depth and spatial relationships, which can vary significantly even with minimal changes in perspective. To address this challenge, our proposed method represents objects in multiple views through a characteristic vector and a rich, diverse dataset that captures the object's appearance from different angles, leveraging a latent style vector to combine these datasets. Our model, which requires only 2D input images and text, generates videos for novel viewpoints in the foreground and background, a task that typically demands extensive 3D information. Experimental results show our approach effectively creates realistic prediction videos for novel scenes and objects, as demonstrated by our quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

An inter-level coupling (ILC) happens when a photon's energy is aligned with the energy difference between two atomic or solid-state levels that differ by a principal quantum number. This type of coupling has numerous implications for recombination processes, radiative transitions, and the formation of atomic states. Although Coulomb interactions can broaden these states, they had not been directly measured in certain applications, such as solid-state physics. We used ultra-cold rubidium atoms in high-lying states to precisely investigate this phenomenon by taking into account the coupling between two very close energy levels, $g_{38}$ and $f_{38}$. A laser-induced transition between these levels and the d state resulted in a transfer of atoms to a trap-lossy state, allowing us to detect this process and its consequences. This discovery opens up the possibility of using laser-controlled inter-level transitions to transfer atoms from s states in solid materials to p states, which could have significant implications for loss mechanisms in rare-earth ion systems.

The Ω-baryon, first predicted by Gell-Mann and Okun, has a rich history that began with theoretical predictions in 1964 and culminated in its discovery at Fermilab in 2010 through analyses of data from fixed target experiments. Due to the limited data available, particularly from the Ω- baryon's rare decay channels, understanding its properties remains challenging. With the LHC running, researchers now have access to vast amounts of strange hadrons produced through pp collisions. A particularly rare decay, Ξ- N̄ X → K- K- K- π+ at 3.1σ, was observed by the CMS collaboration. By analyzing properties of the X resonance, estimates suggest it could be an Ω- baryon with an unexpectedly high mass and strange hadronic molecular configuration. This study involves re-evaluating that mass estimation and producing a more comprehensive evaluation of the X resonance nature, based on the detailed momentum distributions of final-state particles.

Epidemiological studies focusing on infectious transmission in urban bus settings were analyzed with a competitively balanced mathematical model. We used a model that incorporates accurate boundary conditions derived from laboratory ventilation tests to accurately simulate air flow within a enclosed bus environment. Our model demonstrates sufficient accuracy in replicating simulated flow patterns of the bus's ventilation system without the complexity of three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations, and with a level of detail matching three-dimensional simulations but with a level of simplicity comparable to simplified models. Furthermore, our study provides evidence of the value of simplified models that capture the physical dynamics of the surrounding environment in the development of reliable models for epidemiological research and real-time applications.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SPCE) has gained considerable interest within the field of Spintronics due to its potential in lowering the Current-induced Spin-orbit Torque (SOT) threshold. In this study, we investigate the SOT characteristics and SPCE in Cobalt bismuth multilayers to better understand the role of bismuth in inducing spin-orbit effects. A key aspect examined is the interface interaction between the Cobalt and Bismuth layers, and how it influences the SOT properties. By adjusting the order of the layers, we controlled the interface interaction and discovered an inverse relationship between the thickness-dependent decay rate and the Spin Hall angle. Notably, the SPT was observed for the first time in Co/Bi multilayers with strong spin-hall angles exceeding 0.5. These findings highlight the importance of interface interaction and provide valuable insights into engineering multilayer structures with enhanced spin-hall properties.

This research aims to find the exact solutions of the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in multiple dimensions, specifically for a generalised Mie-type potential. The study is conducted within the context of fractional quantum mechanics and involves applying the Jumarie fractional derivative to multiple variables. To achieve this, the Adomian decomposition method is used. The study includes a comprehensive approach to resolving the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation, resulting in a series expansion solution that can be expressed in terms of conformal derivatives. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Adomian decomposition method in providing accurate solutions for the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation, even in multiple dimensions. The study also provides graphical representations of the solutions obtained, offering valuable insights into the behaviour of the system under consideration.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input variations within a specified range, impacts its performance. In our study, we investigated the effects of adding a corresponding penalty to the standard training process. We developed methods to compute the relevant penalty efficiently and incorporated it into various optimization approaches, including gradient descent, an accelerated form of proximal gradient descent, and coordinate descent. Through comprehensive experiments, we found that this penalty enhances the neural network's generalization capabilities, leading to better performance on training data that has experienced some distortion. Furthermore, we discovered that enforcing a certain level of Lipschitz continuity improves the neural network's robustness against adversarial attacks and yields more consistent and acceptable predictions.

We investigate the possibility of observing a signature of a heavy leptoquark through its Drell-Yan production process in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). By taking into account next-to-leading order QCD effects, we found a predicted cross section for a scalar leptoquark of approximately 25 nanobarn and for a fermionic leptoquark of around 30 nanobarn, for a heavy leptoquark with a mass exceeding 800 GeV and decaying into bottom quarks and neutral charm leptons. Given that this predicted cross section can lead to a detectable number of events in experiments searching for such leptoquarks without top quark suppression, it implies that failure to observe such a leptoquark at the LHC would require a broader scope than just the third generation of matter.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images. Nonetheless, current deep-learning approaches have primarily focused on capturing average patterns within large datasets, failing to consider the varying characteristics of data and their impact on model performance. We introduce a novel neural network that adapts to various data distributions jointly training with PET alone and PET combined with MRI, termed Flexible MRI-Uncertainty Aware Neural Network (F-MUANN). Our flexible model can utilize both present and absent MRI data without causing significant performance issues, producing performance-comparable results to existing deep-learning approaches when MRI data is available and offering several unique advantages when MRI data is absent, including accurate neural network predictions and minimal bias in image edges. Our flexible model exhibits exceptional performance both within and outside known data distributions, including scenarios with absent MRI data, as demonstrated in experiments using synthetic and real data, particularly with real data, our model achieves an improvement of 24.1% in peak signal-to-noise ratio and 23.6% in structure similar index in low-dose PET denoising without MRI data.

A linguistic approach known as centering theory (CT) has long been used to predict coreference, but its manual implementation does not scale effectively. Our research introduces a novel application of CT by integrating it into a neural network model, replacing its fundamental elements with vector representations. This innovation allows the algorithm to capture the contextual nuances that dictate pronoun resolution, mirroring the predictions made through traditional CT. Our results demonstrate that our centered attention network (CAN) not only matches the performance of top-tier neural models but also excites with a more efficient and explainable alternative. Can our results match the performance of the very best neural models while providing a more efficient and grounded alternative?

Recently, the application of IEEE 802.11c WiFi technology in indoor navigation and location services has been limited due to its simplicity in protocol but intricacy in implementation. Our approach circumvents the challenging aspects of coaxial cable management by leveraging automated tools for signal capture, filtering, and data processing in WiFi packet analysis. By utilizing machine learning techniques, we developed a fully automatic method for determining the distance of a WiFi access point, including the creation and deployment of mobile applications on both Android and iOS platforms. The resulting system enables the estimation of distances to access points with an average error margin of 2 meters.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for superconducting energy recovery linacs, particularly as beam currents rise. Having divided beam load dependence into static and dynamic components, start load impact was found to match the static component model, while feedback load showed a different pattern. In models with a start load load-dependence similar to IBU's traditional 1+X format was established, but er feedback load a new multiplicative term arose. A novel concept was introduced – the beam filling factor – to account for this multiplicative effect. Demonstration using an actual design showed a 10-fold variation in beam break-up threshold stemming from filling factors alone.

Our main goal is to calculate the one-loop virtual contribution to the two-gluon emission process from a neutral particle in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. To achieve this, we utilize the forward-limit method. Our results can be effectively represented using harmonic polylogarithms with 24 final functions and massless kinematic variables. This allows for a straightforward comparison with two other approaches: the two-particle cut of the $R^4$ term in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ S-matrix expansion, and the two-gluon PDE solution within the $\mathcal{N}=4$ theory. Notably, our results align with the $R^4$ coefficient at one-loop level, consisting of 16 logarithmic functions that define the $r_2$ component of the ERBL operator. Furthermore, we have obtained the two-gluon eikonal phase at one-loop, which can be expressed through 24 harmonic polylogarithms, thereby completing the lowest-order part of the one-loop result in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ theory.

A notable feature recently discovered in highly concentrated polymer solutions within brush configurations is the existence of exclusion regions, where solvent interaction is significantly reduced. This study explores the equilibrium properties and near-surface behavior of complex, short-to-intermediate length polymer solutions, accounting for arbitrary surface arrangements. Using a self-consistent field approach, we analyzed the breakdown of classic brush and train-brush theories in densely packed, stretched molten polymer solutions of simple geometries (planar and cylindrical). We observed a distinct zone near the surface characterized by minimal fluctuation monolayers, followed by a transition zone exhibiting significant exclusion properties. As a result, macromolecules exhibit three distinct regions: a dense layer adjacent to the surface, a zone with limited movement further out, and an outer region exhibiting typical brush characteristics. These observations hold true for both planar and cylindrical configurations regardless of macromolecular architecture (linear or star-shaped). Notably, the existence of exclusion regions is attributed to incompressibility constraints rather than surface geometry, influencing macromolecule behavior and solvent properties. This discovery has significant implications for understanding surface coatings and polymer solutions in a wide array of surface-related industrial processes.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices F can uniquely distinguish between all possible vertex mappings that preserve adjacent and non-adjacent relationships. A smaller measure of precision, known as a trimmed recognition number, is available for practical scenarios where only a certain number of mappings need to be differentiated. A further reduction, called a trimmed metric dimension, averages the size of subsets required to identify a specific number of mappings with the greatest possible distance between them. A study currently explores the properties of this measure in the context of various graph types, including trees and a range of other structures.

A preliminary study was conducted to explore the potential of using a machine learning approach for analyzing full-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The contrast between different types of astronomical objects within these images was found to be significant, and this research reveals that a neural network can effectively distinguish between objects across the entire electromagnetic spectrum within a few minutes on low-specification computer hardware. Research on the varying objects identified objects with unexpected behavior across different time scales, and these findings are discussed in detail within the context of this study.

A convex set of functions is defined as a monarchical structure when when it's supported by extreme elements that're called ministers, and a dominant element is called a monarch.
Recent research reveals the notion of monarchies can be used to develop various approaches for approximating functions, each tailored to a specific type of function family.
This paper introduces a innovative type of approach, and we focus on applying it to the set of polynomials, demonstrating that positive polynomials can be efficiently represented using "semisemic monarchies" with relatively low complexity.
Moreover, our methods allow for comparing and converting monarchies, and we specifically establish that our "semisemic monarchies" can be converted into the well-known "double summonies" previously discovered by other researchers.

We are using optical data from two Pan-STARRS1 image surveys, which encompass a vast 3,000 square degree field, to identify binary asteroids. By employing a novel approach that involves detecting multiple moving objects within the same frame, we found 2,649 binary asteroids moving at speeds below 0.55 degrees per frame. To assess the characteristics of these binary asteroids, we calculated their relative orbital parameters including separation, angular velocity, and the direction of curvature. Unfortunately, our data does not yet enable an assessment of whether certain features, such as comet-like asteroids, are more prevalent in single or binary forms. To better understand the population of binary asteroids, comprehensive spectroscopic analysis is necessary.

This research develops the groundwork for estimating and analyzing the connection between a network and the residual errors of a regression model, with partial linearity. It establishes consistency, efficiency, and confidence intervals through the use of known efficient estimators or by applying network parameters directly in the model. Furthermore, two distinct approaches are introduced: a known-efficiency GMM estimator and a efficient control function method, both of which are valid under different assumptions about parameter identification. The study also explores using these techniques in the context of peer influence through networks, and efficiently evaluates confidence intervals by means of simulation.

This study develops a version of the Leibniz Rule for the interaction between the left-sided Riemann-Liouville variable-order integral and differential operators. The study is particularly interested in applying this technique to the left-sided Riemann-Liouville variable-order differential when both the function and order are non-constant, leading to the establishment of two key reduction theorems under specific conditions. The results obtained in this study build upon previous works that involved constant order integral and differential operators, as well as those that involved a changing (piecewise constant) order differential operator. The proof of our main theorems relies on the application of the left-sided Riemann-Liouville variable-order integral to both polynomial and exponential functions.

The social interactions depicted in the game Dungeons and Dragons involve a dynamic set of relationships between players and the narrative guide, known as the Dungeon Master (DM). To enhance the experience for players, it is crucial to improve the performance of the DM. Our proposed method involves a dmAgent, which mimics the DM's role by guiding the conversation, steering the discussion, and managing the flow of the game. The dmAgent excels at conveying information, managing the flow of the game, and handling the feelings and knowledge of others. It excels in a real-world simulation of the game, surpassing a skilled human DM in guiding the discussion and conveying emotions, and excels in steering the conversation by accurately predicting future discussions and Herculean thoughts. Furthermore, the dmAgent exhibits a robust theory-of-mind, enabling it to accurately foresee future discussions and knowledge based on the Herculean thoughts. It also excels in steering the conversation by predicting future discussions and handling Herculean thoughts. Finally, the dmAgent endorses a strong theory-of-mind, allowing it to predict future discussions and handle Herculean thoughts.

We developed a topological approach to identify realistic bending pathways in knotted proteins. Starting with the native protein structure, our method systematically maps out possible bend locations, taking into account the spatial constraints of the protein. By combining this spatial information with the topological properties of possible loops, we prioritize potential bending sites. We applied this ranked list of possibilities to solve the knotting problem in the Tau-tin protein, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

We define mapping category groups for the symplectic homotopy type, specifically focusing on the blowups of standard tori in various dimensions, which denote the minimal handling costs for a symplectic map to transform one standard torus into another within the same blown-up space.
